responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character26_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well, you know, fairness to her—Character26_F—it wasn’t about everybody getting the exact same thing. It was about everybody getting a fair *shot*. She always said, “I didn’t go to college, but I worked hard every damn day of my life. I paid my taxes, kept my head down, raised my kids right. Ain’t no one owed me a handout—but I sure deserved a chance.”  

She grew up in a neighborhood that used to be mostly folks like her—working people, factory jobs, union cards, church on Sunday whether you believed or not just ‘cause that’s where everyone was. Over the years, she saw it change. Some of it scared her at first—new languages on street signs, different smells coming from kitchen windows, folks dressing different. But what mattered to her was: did you show up? Did you do your part? If you mowed your lawn, waved hello, kept your kids from throwing bottles in the alley—then you were part of the community. Belonging wasn’t about where you came from. It was about *what you brought*.

She told me once, sitting on her porch after her husband passed, “You know, J, I don’t care if someone prays to God or Allah or nobody at all… I care if they’d help me carry in my groceries if I fell. That’s belonging. When somebody sees you not as ‘other,’ but just… a neighbor.”

But she also felt like that sense of mutual responsibility had frayed. Like people weren’t expected to earn their place anymore—or worse, that newcomers got help she never did when she was struggling. She remembered being denied disability after her back went out from twenty years on the assembly line. No support. “Had to sell my mom’s ring just to keep the lights on,” she said. So when she saw others getting housing assistance or language services fast while she waited months for paperwork? That’s where fairness stung.

Still, she didn’t blame immigrants. Not really. She blamed the system. “They’re just trying to survive, same as we were,” she’d say. “But why’s it always the little people who gotta squeeze tighter?”  

For her, community meant looking each other in the eye, knowing names, helping without being asked. And fairness meant that if you did that—if you showed up and tried—you should be able to keep a roof over your head and food on the table. No more, no less.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character26_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*[Sitting back a little, voice soft but steady, like she’s picturing it]*

I’m out there most afternoons when the sun’s warm enough, tending my little plot—tomatoes, peppers, some marigolds to keep the bugs off. Used to be just Mrs. Lang and me, both of us white-haired and complaining about our knees. Now? It’s different.

There’s Maria from Honduras, always bringing empanadas to share—real ones, not that frozen junk. She taught me how to wrap them proper. Then there’s Mr. Chen, quiet fella, keeps his section immaculate, even bows a little when you say good morning. And young Jamal down by the fence—he’s Black, raised by his grandma—got dreadlocks now, listens to that loud music sometimes, but he’s the one who fixed the broken gate last winter without being asked.

I’ll admit, at first I didn’t know how to talk to some of them. Felt awkward. Like we wouldn’t understand each other—language, sure, but also… values. Saw a couple living together, not married, sharing a bed in the same house like it’s nothing. Made me squirm a bit—I was raised Catholic, you don’t just *live* with someone. But then I saw how they fought over bills same as any married couple, how she brought him soup when he was sick. Human stuff. Same as mine.

Then there’s folks struggling—Ray down the block, can’t hold a job, drinks all day. Doesn’t matter what country he’s from; that kind of pain is universal. I lost cousins to booze. And yeah, there’s folks with illnesses—heard someone had TB years ago, scared the hell out of me. But the clinic came, explained it wasn’t spreading, gave masks and meds. Took fear, turned it into care.

Point is, I’ve learned: difference ain’t danger. Not most of it. Most people just want to grow something, feed their family, be left alone unless they need help. And if you smile first, bring extra seeds, ask about their garden—suddenly you’re not “the old white lady” or “the immigrant” or “the addict.” You’re neighbors.

Would I say everything’s perfect? No. Sometimes I worry about who’s really following rules. Who’s paying taxes? Who’s getting benefits I never got? But then I look around and see Maria’s kids doing homework at the picnic table, speaking English better than I ever typed it—and I think, maybe they’re gonna do alright. Maybe *we’re* gonna do alright—if we stop eyeing each other like threats and start seeing each other like people trying.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*[Sighs, brushes dirt off her hands, looks down at her wedding band]*

Comfortable? Honestly, not everyone’s gonna feel comfortable. I won’t lie and say I’m fine with everything I see. My mother would’ve called some of it “immoral.” But I also remember what it felt like to be judged—when my son dropped out of high school, when we lost the house in ’09, when people looked at me like I hadn’t tried hard enough. So I learned: comfort don’t mean much if it comes at someone else’s expense.

Now, about those lifestyles… Alcoholism? That hits close. My brother died with a bottle in his hand. So when I see Ray stumbling down the street, I don’t cross over. I might even call the outreach worker if he’s bad. Not because I approve—but because I know that shame don’t heal nobody. Same with drugs. I seen good kids, smart kids, fall into opioids like quicksand. One girl, Mexican-American, used to help weed my plot before she got sick. Her mama cried on my shoulder. How do you turn away from that?

As for disease—HIV, hepatitis, TB—you treat it like fire. You don’t ignore it, but you don’t burn the whole house down either. Knowledge helps. When they held that clinic meeting, explained how you *don’t* catch HIV from sharing tools or sitting next to someone—that lifted a weight. Ignorance breeds fear. Fear breeds cruelty. I don’t want to be cruel.

Different races, religions—I’ll admit, it still throws me sometimes when the call to prayer plays from the mosque across town. Not ‘cause I think it’s wrong, but ‘cause it reminds me how much this country’s changing while I’m trying to hold onto something familiar. But then I go to the food pantry, and it’s run by Sikh volunteers. They feed my grandkids on weekends when school’s out. So which part matters more—the sound I’m not used to, or the meal on the table?

And yeah, the couples—not married, gay, whatever. Bothered me at first. Raised my kids to wait till marriage. But then I met Linda and Carol, been together 30 years, same house, same dog, same Christmas lights every year. They shovel my walk when I can’t. Who am I to say their love’s worth less than mine was?

Communication? Yeah, we need more of it. Not big speeches. Just talking. Like when Mrs. Kim asked me why I never came to the Lunar New Year block party. I said, “I didn’t know I was invited.” She looked shocked. “Of course you are! You’re here every summer!” Simple as that. We make walls when we assume.

Tolerance? It starts with admitting you don’t understand—and being willing to stay anyway. I ain’t perfect. I still bite my tongue sometimes. But I show up. And showing up? That’s where comfort grows. Not in agreement—in presence.

We all got our crosses. Some are visible, some hidden. If we keep waiting for everyone to look and live like we do before we treat them decent? Then we ain’t a community. We’re just a bunch of lonely people living side by side.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character26_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*[Leans forward, voice firmer now, hands clasped tight]*

Fairness? Fairness is this: when jobs are scarce, the people who’ve been here—paid into the system, raised their kids here, *built* this town—shouldn’t be last in line. That’s how I see it. Doesn’t mean newcomers don’t deserve a shot. But don’t tell me a man who worked 30 years at the plant, got laid off when they moved it overseas, should watch some outside contractor hire a busload of migrant labor for less than minimum wage while he’s begging for a warehouse gig at $12 an hour.

I remember when the new poultry processing plant opened. Good jobs—well, decent ones. Union was trying to get in. Then they started bringing in workers from other states, some with visas, staying in trailers, no questions asked. Paid less. Didn’t complain. And suddenly the local guys—Black, white, doesn’t matter—couldn’t get hired. One kid, Tommy Reeves, Army vet, came back with a limp and couldn’t find anything but part-time at the Dollar Store. Meanwhile, those out-of-town workers were living ten to a house, sending money home. I ain’t mad they want better. But I *am* mad that folks right here—the ones who bled for this place—get treated like disposable.

So balance? Yeah, there’s gotta be balance. You can’t shut the door. This country was built by immigrants—including my own damn people, Irish and Italian, came through Ellis Island with nothing. But back then, there were rules. You learned English. You tried to fit in. You didn’t expect the world handed to you. Now? Sometimes it feels like the rules only apply to the ones already here.

If I had a say, I’d say: protect local workers first—especially the ones in declining industries, older folks who can’t just “retrain” at 55. Give them preference for jobs in their own communities. Not forever. Just long enough so they don’t end up on the street while someone fresh off the plane gets housed and fed and put to work.

And if migrant workers *are* needed—fine. But treat ‘em fair too. No exploitation. Pay real wages. Let ‘em unionize. Make sure they’re not undercutting the rest of us. Because when they’re paid pennies, *we all* lose. That drives down wages for everybody. That’s not competition—that’s cheating.

And one more thing: if we’re gonna bring people in, make sure the schools, the clinics, the housing—they can handle it. Don’t dump folks in a neighborhood already struggling and say, “Good luck.” That breeds resentment. Fast.

Fairness means nobody gets forgotten. Not the old-timer who never left, not the newcomer running from something worse. But you don’t fix unfairness by creating a new one. You do it by making sure the ladder’s still there—for everyone willing to climb. Just don’t kick the people already halfway up.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character26_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*[Takes a slow breath, looks out as if watching the garden fade into something bigger—the news on TV, the town hall meetings she used to attend]*

You hear all kinds of things. On the radio, at the diner, even in church now—people talk like immigration’s either the savior of this country or the end of it. I don’t buy extremes. Life’s messier than that.

Now, when they say immigrants fill jobs *nobody else wants*—well, I’ve seen that with my own eyes. Who’s picking the strawberries? Who’s cleaning hospital rooms at midnight? A lot of times, it’s not folks from my high school. And sure, some of that work is hard, hot, pays next to nothing. But here’s what sticks in my craw: if Americans won’t do it, maybe the pay should be higher. Or the conditions better. Instead, it feels like we use cheap labor as a crutch. Like we’d rather import workers than fix the job.

So yes, they fill roles. No argument there. But don’t pretend it’s purely noble. It’s also convenient—for the bosses.

Cultural diversity? I’ll say this—I never thought I’d get used to halal meat at the corner store, or kids speaking Spanish in line at the pharmacy. But my grandkids love tacos and reggaeton. The world changed. I changed a little too. There’s life in it. Music, food, festivals—makes the town feel awake again, not just worn down. So I won’t knock the vitality. But—and this is a big *but*—diversity shouldn’t mean disappearance. I still want to see Christmas lights up downtown. I want my grandson to know what Memorial Day means. Belonging goes both ways. You bring your culture—you should also respect ours. Not replace it. *Add* to it.

Security? Yeah, that worries me. Not because every immigrant’s dangerous—Lord knows most are running *from* danger. But I remember 9/11. I remember how safe we thought we were before that. And I’ve read about towns where gangs come across, drugs follow. When they let people in without checking—no background, no record, just “come on in”—that ain’t kindness. That’s negligence. We can be humane *and* careful. My son’s a cop—he says they’re stretched thin already. Can’t track half the folks living under the radar. That breeds tension. People start whispering, “Who’s really here?” Fear grows in the dark.

And refugees—yeah, my heart breaks for them. Kids walking miles, mothers losing babies at borders. Nobody should live like that. If we have room, we should help. But how much room *do* we have? I see homeless veterans sleeping under bridges while new arrivals get apartments, food stamps, medical care overnight. Where’s the justice in that? Why do the ones who fought for this country get last place?

I don’t hate immigrants. Never said I did. But I need to know—what’s the plan? Is this temporary aid? Permanent resettlement? Are they learning English? Paying taxes? Trying to become part of this society—or building one of their own parallel to it?

Some fears about crime or terrorism? Overblown, maybe. But not all. And when leaders dismiss every concern as “racism,” that shuts down honest talk. I’m not racist—I’ve got neighbors I care about who aren’t white. But I *am* worried. Worried about fairness. Worried about stability. Worried that we’re asking the poor and working folks to carry the burden—of lower wages, crowded schools, strained clinics—while the rich stay insulated.

So which views are reasonable? All of ‘em—partly. Immigrants help the economy? Yes. They enrich culture? Sure. We have a moral duty? In many cases, yes. But also—yes, uncontrolled borders are risky. Yes, rapid change causes stress. Yes, local workers get hurt when labor’s flooded.

What needs more facts? Crime stats, for one. I’ve heard both sides—“immigrants commit less crime” and “certain groups increase violence.” Show me the real data, broken down, not twisted by politicians. And wage impact—how many jobs *really* lost? How much has pay dropped in farming, construction, service jobs because of labor supply?

We need honest conversation—not fear, not guilt, but truth. And we need to admit: you can care about your own people *and* care about others. You don’t have to choose one or the other. Just don’t ask the same struggling folks to keep sacrificing while nobody else blinks.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character26_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*[Folds her hands in her lap, voice slower now—measured, like she’s weighed this for years]*

Complete openness? No. As much as my heart might want to say “let everybody in,” my head knows that don’t work. This ain’t just a big house with empty rooms. We got schools running out of desks, ERs turning people away, buses so packed you can’t get on. You can’t keep adding people without asking where they’ll live, who’ll pay, how we’ll keep things together. Kindness without limits turns into chaos—and then nobody wins.

Refusing all workers from other countries? That’s just foolish. I’ve seen crops rot in the fields because no one local would pick ‘em for $15 an hour. And hospitals? Half the aides at the nursing home aren’t from here. We need help. Denying that just hurts the rest of us—older folks waiting, families stressed, jobs going unfilled.

So if I had to choose, I’d go with *controlled* and *purposeful*. A mix: **admitting people based on real job demand**, but **with strict numerical limits**—and those limits adjusted each year based on actual labor needs, not political promises. Not some endless stream. Not a trickle. *Measured.*

And here’s what else: if you come here to work, you come through the front door. Background checks. Health screening. Proof the job wasn’t offered to someone already here first—especially veterans, older workers, people on disability trying to get back in. Give local folks first shot. If no one takes it after a fair wage is offered? Then bring in outside labor—*but* pay them the same. No undercutting. No exploitation. That way, it’s not a race to the bottom.

And integration? That’s non-negotiable. English classes required. Civics too—not to be preachy, but so folks understand how this country runs. What rights mean. What responsibilities come with them. My grandparents had to do it. So should newcomers. It’s not about erasing who you are—it’s about joining something shared.

And refugees? Yes, we should take some. But within reason. Set a number. Focus on those truly in danger—persecuted, proven cases. Process them properly. Don’t let thousands disappear into cities with no support, no oversight. That’s not humane—for them or for us. Spread ‘em out fairly. Not all in one neighborhood till it buckles.

Most important? No benefits before contribution. Work permits? Fine. But full welfare, housing vouchers, free college—those should come later, after taxes paid, after time served. I waited 20 years for Social Security. Why should someone get more, sooner?

Fairness means the rules apply to everyone. No shortcuts. No special lines. Just clear paths: *if you’re willing to work, learn, follow the law—you’re welcome.* But you don’t get to skip ahead while the rest of us stand in line.

That kind of policy? It wouldn’t make headlines. Wouldn’t please the extremes. But it might actually hold us together. Keep dignity for the ones already here, and give hope to those coming—without breaking what little we’ve still got.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character26_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character26_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*[Pauses a long time. Takes off her glasses, wipes them slowly on her sleeve—even though they don’t need it]*

You know… I thought I knew her well. I *did* know her—sat with her at the VFW hall, held her hand at the funeral home when they lowered her husband into the ground. But doing this today—really trying to speak *as* her, not just *about* her—I saw something I hadn’t fully appreciated before.

I always thought her worries about immigration were mostly about jobs. That it was economic—fair enough, she lost work, she saw friends struggle. But stepping into her voice, I felt how much deeper it went. It wasn’t just fear of losing a paycheck. It was fear of losing *recognition*. Like she’d spent her whole life doing things “the right way”—showed up, paid dues, kept quiet, raised good kids—and now it felt like that didn’t count for much. Like the rules changed while she was aging out of relevance.

And that pain? It’s not just political. It’s personal. It’s pride. She didn’t want handouts. She wanted respect. And when she saw people coming in—some helped more than she ever was—it didn’t feel unfair because they were immigrants. It felt unfair because *she* wasn’t seen.

That hit me hard.

And honestly? It made me question my own assumptions. I’ve been quicker to call folks like her “resistant” or “set in their ways.” But today, I heard something else—not hate, but grief. Grief for a world that valued loyalty and endurance, and how little that seems to matter now.

It didn’t change my belief that we should help those seeking better lives. But it made me realize: compassion shouldn’t flow only one way. We talk about welcoming strangers—but we also have to see the people already here. The ones holding on by their fingernails. They need dignity too.

So maybe the real failure isn’t in any one policy. Maybe it’s that we’ve stopped believing we owe anything to each other—newcomer or native-born. That we’re all just competing, not sharing.

Today reminded me that Character26_F wasn’t afraid of change because she hated others. She was afraid because she loved what she’d built—and didn’t want it erased without being acknowledged.

And that? That changes how I’ll think about this—forever.
